newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition throws down gauntlet to Kohl.
newsitem.headline: German opposition throws down gauntlet to Kohl.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) threw down the gauntlet to Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Friday, demanding he speed up the tax cuts at the heart of his reelection strategy or see the planned reform fail.

SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine, clearly trying to wrong-foot Kohl while the centre-right government is split over long-overdue economic reforms, said the 1999 tax cut target date aimed only at winning votes in next year's general election.
"Either we agree on a clear tax cut for 1998 or you can forget it," said Lafontaine, whose party can block legislation thanks to its majority in the upper house of parliament.
Kohl, who wanted draw out the controversial reform debate for months until a consensus emerged, had earlier appealed for all-party discussions on his government's plans.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel responded to Lafontaine with an offer of early tax cuts, but hedged this with conditions that would make it difficult for the SPD to accept.

Kohl called the debate on the German economy after the cornerstone of his political strategy this year -- the long-overdue reform of the tax and pension systems -- got bogged down in bitter rows within his own coalition.

Doubts about Kohl's leadership have also been mounting as younger leaders among his Christian Democrats (CDU) openly grumbled and his loyal crown prince Wolfgang Schaeuble unexpectedly said he wanted to become chancellor one day.
Kohl, with 14 years in office Bonn's longest-serving chancellor, has not said whether he will seek reelection in the October 1998 vote but Bonn insiders expect him to do so.

The "fighting speech" Kohl planned to regain the political upper hand was a spirited defence of his policies, which he said would lead to 2.5 percent economic growth this year and a drop in the record number of 4.1 million unemployed.
But the address contained no new initiatives. Kohl reminded management and labour they had also agreed with him to try to create jobs and halve unemployment by the year 2000.

Kohl, 66, also urged the opposition, business, trade unions and the churches to join in a year-long public debate on pensions, even though his own party is split over whether to raise value-added tax to finance reform.
"Only at the end of this discussion can we decide about the necessary financing," he said. "Then we will see who has the better ideas."
Taking up the SPD challenge, Waigel said tax reform could be passed by August and implented in January.
But for this he demanded the opposition accept his plan as the basis for negotiation and pledge not to use its majority in the upper house of parliament to force through a compromise.
Kohl's Free Democrat (FDP) partners, who have been calling for far more tax cuts than Waigel thinks he can finance, promptly seconded the call for an earlier tax reform.
The SPD says the tax plan, which is to cut overall tax revenues by 30 billion marks ($18.28 billion), will not bring real relief to most workers because tax breaks will be cut.
Scrapping a wealth tax and dropping top tax rates from 53 to 39 percent will also give far more to the rich than the middle class, the main opposition party argues.
Kohl blamed part of the unemployment problem on the fact more women and foreigners were seeking jobs in a tight market.
Women had taken two million of the three million new jobs created in western Germany in the past eight years, he said.
Moreover in 1995, Germany had taken in more immigrants than the United States -- 1.1 million compared to 720,000. Germans were also refusing to take jobs that foreigners ended up doing.
"This has enormous consequences," he said.
Greens party leader Joschka Fischer warned Kohl not to start blaming foreigners for Germany's unemployment problem, saying: "You will stoke up racial tension like that."
Labour Minister Norbert Bluem, under fire in the coalition for his pension reform proposals, also defended his ideas and urged the opposition to seek a consensus with him.

Bluem, the last remining member from Kohl's first cabinet in 1982, has threatened to resign if the government rejects his plans to cut pension benefits, raise contributions and jack up VAT to help pay for other programmes like child benefits.
